mech: A drier, more seasonal climate broke the forest into savanna patches where yam, oil-palm and pearl-millet farmers could settle and move on.
A language phylogeny mapped on vegetation shows speakers moved fast through savanna and paused for centuries at forest edges: habitat set the route and the pace.
Genomes of southern and eastern Bantu speakers trace back to West-Central Africa south of the rainforest, a late split after the forest crossing.
An eastern stream of iron-using farmers moved down the woodlands from the Great Lakes into southern Africa.
Iron hoes and axes made it faster to clear woodland and open new fields, so farming villages could multiply eastward.
Grains and cattle borrowed from Sudanic and Cushitic neighbours let Bantu farmers leave the wet forests for drier eastern savannas.
Moving farmers married into forager and herder communities rather than simply replacing them.
Many small moves, not one wave, carried a shared political vocabulary of house, village and district across the forest.
Over many centuries, houses and districts were aggregated into chiefdoms and then the kingdoms of West Central Africa.
Early Iron Age farmers brought the cattle-and-grain economy whose herds later became the wealth of plateau elites.
When Mapungubwe declined in the 1200s, its sacred, class-divided kingship and its trade links moved north to the plateau.
Herds that could be lent, given and moved between highveld and lowveld built the followings of plateau chiefs.
Control of gold and ivory leaving for the coast paid for the imported beads, cloth and porcelain found in the elite enclosures.
The biggest walls went up in the 1300s and 1400s, when the coastal trade was at its height and labour could be mobilised.
Kilwa’s sultans grew rich by controlling the Sofala gold that came down from the plateau.
The Portuguese attacked Kilwa and built a fort at Sofala to seize the gold trade at its outlet.
Firewood, grazing and fertile soil near the capital ran out, and a town that size could not move its food supply far.
When gold began to move along the Zambezi, Great Zimbabwe lost the tribute that had paid for its elite.
The elite and its building tradition carried on at Khami and in the Mutapa state rather than vanishing.
Karl Mauch’s 1871 claim that the ruins were the Queen of Sheba’s palace gave settlers a biblical origin story to repeat.
Rhodes’ company paid for Bent’s 1891 dig and needed a past in which Africans had not built anything worth owning.
Believing the African layers were later squatters’ rubbish, Hall dug them away and destroyed the evidence that would have dated the site.
The controversy brought the British Association to send a trained excavator, who found only African material.
Settlers kept rejecting Randall-MacIver, so the British Association sent another excavation in 1929 to settle it.
A settler state that justified minority rule could not afford a great African past, so it leaned on museums and guidebooks.
After UDI in 1965 the regime treated the question of who built the ruins as a political one.
The harder the regime denied the site’s African builders, the more nationalists made it their symbol and their country’s name.
Mali sat between the Bambuk and Bure goldfields and the Sahelian markets, and taxed the gold as it moved north.

view: D. T. Niane (griot tradition); Michael Gomez
mech: Sunjata’s victory united the Mande clans under one mansa and gave the empire its founding charter.
Towns on the Middle Niger were already trading iron, copper, fish and grain long before Arab merchants arrived, so the Saharan trade grafted onto an African network.
Caravans brought salt, copper, horses and books south and took gold north, and the mansas took a share of everything.
Islam gave Mali’s rulers literate officials, diplomatic standing and trust with North African merchants.
The hajj was statecraft: a display of wealth and piety that put Mali on the map of the Islamic world.
Musa and his retinue spent and gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value against silver fell.
Stories of the golden king reached Mediterranean traders, and Majorcan mapmakers put him on the world map.
Musa came home with scholars and the poet-architect al-Sahili, and Timbuktu got its great mosque.
Royal patronage of mosques and scholars helped make Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.
Europe was short of gold, so a sea route to West African gold was worth the risk and expense.
The image of a golden king beyond the desert helped set Portuguese captains looking for Guinea gold.
Akan gold that once went north to the Niger began to be sold at the coast for cloth, brass and slaves.
The first Portuguese slave trading in the Gulf of Guinea carried captives from Benin to sell to Akan gold merchants at Elmina.
With less gold coming over the desert, Morocco’s sultan decided to seize the source by force.
Ahmad al-Mansur sent his musketeers across the Sahara to take the land of gold and pay for his state.
As Mali’s court fought over succession, Gao broke away and Songhay rulers built their own empire on the middle Niger.
A shrinking Mali survived as a Mande kingdom for two more centuries before breaking up.
Moroccan guns broke the Songhay army and the empire split into smaller states.
Plantations needed more labour than Native captives could supply, so Brazil became the largest single destination of the trade.
Caribbean sugar made the shipping of goods, captives and sugar a regular commercial circuit.
Expanding Caribbean and Brazilian plantations drove embarkations to their eighteenth-century peak.
In the late 1780s French ships landed tens of thousands of captives a year in Saint-Domingue alone.

view: Herbert Klein; David Eltis and David Richardson
mech: Crowding, bad water and dysentery killed roughly one captive in seven at sea, less in the later centuries.
As the Taíno died, Spanish colonists sought African labour; the crown licensed direct shipments from Africa in 1518.
Cuba’s sugar boom kept slave ships coming for decades after Britain banned the trade.
British abolition became a naval campaign, and Royal Navy pressure in Brazilian waters forced Brazil’s 1850 ban.
The wars that broke up Oyo sent Yoruba captives to Bahia and Cuba in the last decades of the trade.
Once a captive could be sold for imported goods, kidnapping, raiding and selling people through rigged courts paid.
Guns were among the leading goods paid for captives.
A gun-slave cycle: states bought guns to raid for captives and to defend themselves from raiders who had guns.
Kongo’s wars were about the throne; their prisoners were sold because a market existed, not the other way round.
The money to be made selling prisoners gave rival factions a reason to keep fighting.
Kongo’s open succession rules let rival royal houses each claim the throne once the king fell at Mbwila.
The restored kingdom stayed decentralised, and its provinces kept fighting through the eighteenth century.
Dahomey conquered the coast to deal with European buyers directly instead of through Allada and Ouidah middlemen.
Exports took mostly young men and women; with deaths in raids and marches added, losses outran births in the hardest-hit regions.
Exports were a small share of West Africa’s people and were offset by births, so the trade slowed growth rather than reversing it.
Maize and cassava raised food output and helped African populations absorb losses that would otherwise have been deeper.
Portuguese ships carried American crops to the African coast, and African farmers spread them inland.
Supplying the Atlantic built networks of raiders, markets and owners that turned slavery into a central institution.
Jihad captives were settled on plantations around Sokoto and Kano, making the caliphate a giant slave society.
The palm oil and groundnuts that replaced the slave trade were often produced and carried by enslaved workers.
With the British market for captives closed, West African merchants and rulers turned to vegetable oils.
Raiding between and within villages kept political units small and set communities against each other.
Fragmented societies built weaker states after colonial rule, and weak states are poor.
Across 52 countries, more slaves exported (per area) predicts lower income in 2000, and the places hit hardest were not poorer to begin with.
Where neighbours and kin had sold each other, distrust became a cultural rule passed down the generations.
Captives paid for cheap imported cloth and metal, and local craft industries lost the chance to grow.
Africa entered the colonial era without the manufacturing base that might have let it industrialise.
In famine years people were pawned, sold or sold themselves, and refugees became easy prey for raiders.
Temperature shocks raised local mortality and cut the cost of supplying captives, and exports from the affected ports moved with them.
Africans’ forced labour in the Americas created the Atlantic markets and raw cotton that pulled British manufacturing into mass production.
Profits of the triangular trade financed British industry; critics reply that the profits were too small to matter much.
A mass movement made the trade politically indefensible even though it was still profitable: econocide.
Williams argued the British Caribbean sugar economy was in decline, so abolition followed interest; Drescher showed it was still growing.
The revolution frightened planters and showed what slavery cost, but its push on British abolition was indirect and double-edged.

view: J. A. Hobson; V. I. Lenin
mech: Underconsumption at home left capital seeking higher returns abroad, and investors pushed governments to secure territories.
Ismail borrowed heavily for the canal and his modernising projects, and in 1875 sold Egypt’s canal shares to Britain.
European control of Egypt’s budget, with army cuts and foreign officials, provoked a proto-nationalist reaction.
London read ʿUrabi as a threat to the Suez route to India and invaded.
The occupation protected British bondholders and trade in Egypt; strategy was the language, money the interest.
The canal made Egypt the hinge of the route to India, which the official mind would not risk.
France, shut out of Egypt, pushed harder in West Africa and the Congo, and the other powers raced to keep up.
Falling prices strained African rulers and European merchants, who began to call for colonial control of the trade.
Many small producers entered the oil trade, so falling world prices hit a large and politically restless group.
Before quinine, European troops died so fast in West Africa that inland conquest was out of reach.
Quinine prophylaxis cut European deaths enough to make inland expeditions affordable.
Small columns with breech-loaders and machine guns could defeat much larger African armies, which made conquest cheap.
Maxim guns and rifles killed about 10,000 Mahdist soldiers for fewer than 50 dead on Kitchener’s side.
Rinderpest killed most of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa, and famine weakened societies just as invaders arrived.
Rival claims on the Congo and the coast led Bismarck to call the powers to Berlin to set rules for claiming land.
The powers recognised Leopold’s International Association as the sovereign of the Congo basin.
A state run for profit made rubber a tax in kind and enforced quotas with hostages and the chicotte.
Killings, flight, hunger and lost births from forced labour emptied whole districts.
Casement himself gave sleeping sickness a prominent place among the causes of the decline he saw.
Men away collecting rubber could not clear fields, and food was requisitioned for posts.
Rules for claiming coasts and spheres led to borders drawn with little knowledge of who lived where.
Partitioned groups face discrimination on both sides of the line and see more political violence.
Italy’s push from Eritrea met Menelik II’s army, which had bought modern rifles and won.
French columns from Senegal ran into the largest state of the western Sudan, which fought back for sixteen years.
German forced cotton growing and taxes drove peoples of southern Tanganyika into a rebellion that cost tens of thousands of lives in war and famine.
A British punitive expedition burned Benin City and carried off thousands of its bronzes and ivories.
Planters worked people to death and replaced them with new captives, so the enslaved stayed mostly African-born.
Kongo’s wars sold trained soldiers to French slavers, so many of Saint-Domingue’s Africans had fought before.
African veterans brought small-unit tactics and ideas of kingship and legitimate rule into the insurgent bands.
The fight between planters, free people of colour and Paris over the Rights of Man split the colony’s rulers and opened the way.
Maroon bands and Vodou gatherings gave the enslaved the networks and leaders to rise together.
Short of troops against Spain, Britain and the insurgents, the commissioners turned to emancipation to win Black soldiers.
Deputies elected in Saint-Domingue carried the fact of emancipation to Paris, and the Convention abolished slavery everywhere.
Abolition brought Toussaint over from Spain to the Republic, and his army became France’s in the colony.
Toussaint built the disciplined army and state that Dessalines would lead to independence.
News that Napoleon had restored slavery in Guadeloupe turned a war over French authority into a war for freedom and independence.
Tens of thousands of non-immune European soldiers arrived in the rainy season among Aedes mosquitoes.
Yellow fever killed most of the French army, including Leclerc, while the largely immune insurgents waited it out.
Without Saint-Domingue, Louisiana was useless to Napoleon, and he sold it for war money.
The collapse of the world’s largest sugar producer sent prices up and Cuban planters into the gap.
France refused recognition until a fleet in 1825 forced Haiti to pay former colonists for their lost property.
Loans from French banks to pay the indemnity drained Haiti’s revenues for generations.
The free Black republic was the one place a defeated Bolívar could rearm, and Pétion asked for emancipation in return.
A revolution contemporaries thought impossible was boycotted diplomatically and then left out of the story of the age of revolutions.
Ships brought Old World pathogens to people with no prior exposure; smallpox reached Hispaniola by 1518.
Forced labour in gold mines, separated families and disrupted farming crushed births and raised deaths before any epidemic.
The smallpox of 1518 killed a large share of the Taíno who had survived the first quarter century.
Smallpox crossed from Cuba to Mexico with the Narváez expedition in 1520.
The first smallpox epidemic killed perhaps a third or more of central Mexico’s people in a year.
Cocoliztli of 1545 was the deadliest single epidemic, killing millions of Native people within a few years.
The epidemic struck during extreme drought, which may have helped a rodent-borne or local pathogen spread.
DNA from victims at Teposcolula-Yucundaa contains Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, a likely culprit that may have arrived from Europe.
The second great cocoliztli again followed severe drought.
A second wave took close to half of the survivors.
Forced labour, enslavement, famine and displacement made people far more likely to die when epidemics came.
Epidemics reached the Andes ahead of Pizarro and returned in waves through the century.
The mining draft killed and scattered men; whole families fled their communities to avoid it.
Las Casas and other friars made the abuses of encomienda a scandal at court.
Slave raiding, war and refugee crowding created the conditions in which the 1696-1700 smallpox epidemic swept the region.
Dobyns argued epidemics spread from de Soto’s army and emptied the chiefdoms long before English traders arrived.
With nine in ten farmers gone, terraces and fields were abandoned and forest grew back.
Abandoned Andean and Amazonian fields reverted to woodland.

view: Simon Lewis and Mark Maslin; Alexander Koch
mech: Regrowing forests and fewer fires pulled carbon out of the air; the ice cores show CO2 bottoming out around 1610.
The CO2 drop added a small cooling of about 0.15 C to the coldest phase of the Little Ice Age; solar and volcanic forcing did more.
Cold, failed harvests and extreme weather in the mid-seventeenth century fed famine, revolt and war across Eurasia.
A hegemonic empire ruled through tribute, not garrisons, and left unconquered enemies like Tlaxcala on its doorstep.
Tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors, porters and boat-builders fought the siege; the Spaniards were a small spearhead.
Steel blades, armour, horses and guns let a few hundred Spaniards survive battles against far larger armies.
Smallpox killed the new emperor Cuitlahuac and many defenders in the months between the Spanish flight and the siege.
Tlaxcala tested the newcomers in battle, found them useful, and chose to use them against the Mexica.
The conquest removed the Mexica overlords, but the local city-states kept running their own affairs.
Spanish chroniclers, and Nahua writers explaining defeat, invented the story that Moctezuma thought Cortés a god.
Warmer centuries and tree planting raised yields around Cusco, freeing labour and food for armies.
The expanding state organised conquered peoples into rotating labour service and stocked storehouses along the roads.
An epidemic killed Huayna Capac and his chosen heir, leaving Huascar and Atahualpa to fight for the throne.

view: John Hemming; Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa
mech: Atahualpa, fresh from victory and on his way to Cusco, met Pizarro with his guard rather than his army.
Horses, steel and surprise let 168 Spaniards kill thousands of unarmoured attendants and seize the Inca.
Peoples crushed by Atahualpa’s generals or recently conquered by the Inca saw the Spaniards as allies.
With Atahualpa held and then killed, Pizarro marched on Cusco with Huascar’s partisans.
Andean allies helped the Spaniards survive the siege of Cusco and hunt down the Vilcabamba Incas.
A generation of conquest, epidemics and broken alliances left Andean people ready to believe the huacas would return.
Taki Onqoy preachers blamed the epidemics on neglect of the huacas.
Millenarian unrest and the Vilcabamba state convinced Spanish authorities that the Andes needed a thorough reorganisation.
Toledo built the mining draft on the Inca habit of rotating labour service, turned to a new purpose.
Spanish bellows failed on Potosí ore, so Native smelters used their own wind furnaces and kept much of the silver.
The first boom of the 1540s and 1550s ran on Indigenous know-how and wage-seeking migrants.
Amalgamation needed mercury in bulk, and a nearby mine made the patio process pay at Potosí.
Mercury amalgamation could process the low-grade ore left after the rich surface veins ran out, and output multiplied.
Drafted labour came at a fraction of its cost, subsidising the mine owners through the great boom.
Mitayos, their families, free workers and traders made the mining camp one of the biggest cities of the Americas.
Refiners trod mercury into ore with bare feet and burned it off in open ovens, poisoning workers and the city.
Miners at Huancavelica breathed mercury vapour and dust in the shafts.
Inside the mita boundary, haciendas were few, land titles weak and roads poor, and the gap persists in consumption and children’s growth.
More money chasing the same goods: Spanish prices tracked treasure imports.
Prices were rising before American silver arrived in quantity; more people and faster-circulating money in growing towns drove grain prices up.
A tax system run in silver made silver worth about twice as much in China as in Europe, and the galleons carried the arbitrage.
Ming officials could only commute taxes into silver because Japanese and American silver was already flowing in.
With Manila founded, silver from Acapulco met Chinese junks every year: the birth of continuous world trade.
A large share of Potosí’s silver ended up in China, by the Pacific or round the Cape.
Less silver meant deflation, harder tax payments and unpaid soldiers in the empire’s last decade; von Glahn doubts imports fell that much.
Unusually wet centuries boosted harvests and populations and let kingdoms multiply.

view: David Webster; B. L. Turner and Jeremy Sabloff
mech: Millions of farmers and lime kilns for plaster cleared forests and pushed farming onto erodible slopes.

view: B. L. Turner and Jeremy Sabloff
mech: Clearing forest may have cut local rainfall and made droughts worse.
Cariaco Basin and lake sediments show multi-year droughts around 810, 860 and 910, matching waves of abandonment.
A rainfall drop of only about a quarter to two-fifths was enough, because summer storms that filled reservoirs failed first.
Societies already near the limits of their land had no reserves when harvests failed.
Crowded kingdoms competed for land and labour.
As rainfall fell after 660, carved records of warfare rose.
Dos Pilas’ aggressive dynasty overreached, and its subject cities turned on it.
In the Petexbatún, war broke the region apart decades before the worst droughts, so drought cannot be the whole story.

view: Arthur Demarest; Simon Martin and Nikolai Grube
mech: Endless rivalry among holy lords drained labour and tribute and eroded the ideology of divine kings.
Kings who claimed to bring rain through ritual lost credibility when the rains failed.
When royal authority failed, the carving of dated stelae stopped; Tikal’s last is from 869.
What collapsed was a political system: commoners stopped supporting courts and drifted away.

view: Patricia McAnany and Norman Yoffee; James Aimers
mech: Power, people and trade shifted to the northern lowlands and the coasts, where Chichen Itza flourished.

view: James Aimers; Patricia McAnany and Norman Yoffee
mech: The southern city-states ended, but Maya society reorganised elsewhere rather than disappearing.
Six centuries without big floods let farmers settle and plant the rich floodplain of the American Bottom.
Warm, moist growing seasons in the Medieval Climate Anomaly favoured maize on the Mississippi.
Surplus maize fed a sudden gathering of tens of thousands of people around a new ceremonial centre.
Cahokia’s rulers and priests mobilised labour to raise Monks Mound and level the Grand Plaza.
Drier growing seasons cut maize yields and storage, undermining the chiefs who redistributed food.
A great flood around 1200 swamped fields and storage in the bottomlands just as decline began.
Faecal stanols in lake mud track people leaving as summer rain fell, after the flood.
Food stress may have turned rivals violent, and the centre walled itself in.
The wall speaks of rising conflict and a political order that was fragmenting.
Milner’s lower estimate: a dispersed farming population of thousands, not a city of 40,000.
